transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Lee. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Lee. Well, what brought me in is... I just can't stop jumping out of my skin lately. I do maintenance and repair work, and if a breaker snaps loud, or a guy drops a tool, or even if somebody just comes up behind me, I completely overreact. 

And it's not just a quick flinch, either. My heart just starts hammering in my chest, and it keeps pounding long after everyone else has just moved on and gone back to work. It's just... it's getting to be too much, and I need to figure out how to get it to stop.
Did this jumpy, heart-pounding reaction start after any particular frightening, dangerous, or traumatic event happened to you, or has it developed more gradually without a clear triggering incident?
Yeah, it definitely started after a specific incident. This has all been going on since an arc-flash accident I had on a retrofit job. That was... I'd say about a year and a month ago now.
Since the accident, have you had unwanted memories, flashbacks, or nightmares where you feel like you're re-living the arc-flash event?

Yeah, I do. It happens out of nowhere, honestly. I could just be doing something normal, like loading tools in the truck, and suddenly I'll see that flash in my head again. Or I'll hear the trainee yelling. It just... it knocks me sideways. It really feels like it's happening all over again right in that moment.

latest_inference.note: Symptoms began after a specific traumatic event (arc-flash accident) 13 months ago, with intrusive flashbacks, hyperarousal, and exaggerated startle response persisting well beyond 1 month, which rules out Acute Stress Disorder (F43.21) and is inconsistent with GAD (F41.1) given the clear trauma-linked re-experiencing symptoms. This presentation is consistent with PTSD.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient developed a cluster of symptoms directly following a specific, identifiable traumatic event (an arc-flash accident) approximately 13 months ago. Symptoms include intrusive re-experiencing (flashbacks, unwanted memories triggered by sensory cues), marked physiological hyperarousal (exaggerated startle response, prolonged heart pounding after triggers), and significant functional distress at work. The chronicity (>1 month, now over a year), clear trauma linkage, and combination of re-experiencing plus hyperarousal symptoms meet criteria for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder, chronic type (F43.10), rather than Acute Stress Disorder (too long duration) or Adjustment Disorder (symptoms are trauma-specific and intrusive rather than general distress) or Generalized Anxiety Disorder (anxiety is trauma-triggered, not diffuse worry).
